chunk_findings.detail: `item_completed` now closes the item's bugs *before* the completion verdict is evaluated, and never rolls those closures back when the verdict refuses. Concretely: let `T` be a fix task whose pipeline is incomplete for an unrelated reason (say a required changelog/coverage step), and `B` a bug with `B.open and B.fix_task == T`. Running `item completed T --regression-test tests/test_x.py::test_y` calls `bug_fixed(repo, B, regression_test=[...])`, which succeeds and persists `B` as closed (and reloads `log/cfg/st`), and only afterwards does the code reach `if not v.may_complete and not force: return O.refused(...)`. The user gets a refusal for `T`, but `B` is already gone from the open queue even though its fix task never completed. This contradicts requirement (b) ("the bug closes when that task completes with a verified regression test") — closure is keyed to the *call*, not to a successful completion. The docstring's justification ("the bug IS fixed and tested; the item's pipeline is another matter") only holds when the refusal is not itself about the fix/test pipeline, and in any case leaves a closed bug with an open, possibly-abandoned fix task and no rule to reopen or re-check it. Note also that because the closures are applied before the verdict, a second `item completed T` invocation (after the pipeline is fixed) reports `bugs_closed: []`, silently hiding the fact that the closure already happened on a refused run.

chunk_findings.detail: `_fix_task_of` decides that `item` "is the task that is fixing" the bug whenever the item is an open task that `branch_kind(it, cfg)` does not classify as a feature — it never checks that the task is actually a bug fix (e.g. that its tag is in `cfg.flow.bugfix_tags` or that it carries `fixes`). The handler only reaches `_file_fix_task` when `prior is None`, i.e. for a brand-new bug, so `item` is the item the bug was *found in*, not a pre-existing fix for this bug. Concretely: `ddflow bug found --item task-42 --summary "..."` where `task-42` is an ordinary open task (not a feature, not a bugfix) makes `_fix_task_of` return `task-42`, so `_file_fix_task` returns `{"fix_task": "task-42", "filed": False}` and never appends `task.added` for `fix-<bid>`. The reply reports `fix_task=task-42, fix_task_filed=false`, and the bug is linked to an unrelated task; when `task-42` completes there is no fix task carrying the required regression test, so the default "bug found creates a fix task" and the regression-test gate (b) are both bypassed. The exception was intended only for the dedupe's `filed_against` case, but that path returns earlier and never reaches `_file_fix_task`, so in practice this branch turns *any* open in-progress task into a bogus fix.

chunk_findings.detail: The bugs are closed *before* the completion verdict is evaluated, and the closures survive a refusal. `bug_fixed(...)` is called and the bug is recorded as fixed, then `services.completion` is consulted; if `v.may_complete` is false and `force` is not set, the function returns `O.refused(...)` — but the bug is already closed. Concretely: bug B has fix task T; the agent runs `item completed T --regression-test tests/test_b.py` but omits, say, the changelog entry. `bug_fixed` closes B, the verdict refuses, and the reply is a refusal while B is no longer open. T is still open and its pipeline incomplete; if T is later abandoned (or completed with `--force` and no test), B stays closed with no completed fix, which is exactly the "bugs over bugs" / "closes when that task completes" property the intent (b) requires. The docstring's "the bug IS fixed and tested; the item's pipeline is another matter" is the change justifying its own behavior, but it contradicts the stated requirement that the bug closes on *completion*, so any refusal path leaves a falsely-closed bug with no regression guard in the queue.

chunk_findings.detail: The helper's docstring promises that when the fix task is kept ("somebody has claimed, or that fixes a real bug too ... the reply names it and the agent decides"), but the only new field in the outcome is `fix_task_removed=removed`, and `removed` is `""` in exactly that case. Given bug B whose fix task T is leased (`t.lease` truthy) or shared with another open bug, `bug invalid B` returns `fix_task_removed=""`, which is byte-for-byte identical to the "B had no fix task" result. The caller is never told that T is still queued or which task it is, so the promised "agent decides" is impossible: it cannot distinguish "nothing was left behind" from "T is still in the DAG".

chunk_findings.detail: The new ordering writes the bug event — including `fix_task = fix-<bid>` — *before* `_file_fix_task` actually creates that task, and the only recovery the comment cites is the separate migration command `bug file-tasks`. That command is described in the intent as a one‑shot upgrade migration and nothing in `bug found`, `next` or `plan` invokes it, so the natural retry path no longer heals the state. Concretely: if `_file_fix_task` raises after the `bug.found` event has been durably appended (the code's own premise: "the lock is no rollback (each append is durable on its own)"), the command aborts with `B` recorded open and `fix_task=fix-B` pointing at a task that was never filed. Re‑running `bug found B` cannot repair it, because `prior = st.bugs.get(B)` is now non‑None, so `filing` is False, `linked` is empty and `_file_fix_task` is never called again — the bug is permanently without its fix task until an operator manually runs the migration. Under the old order the same crash (task appended, bug event not yet written) self‑healed: on retry `prior` was still None, `_file_fix_task` ran idempotently, found the already‑live `fix-B` via `_has_fix_task`, and the bug event was then written linking it. So the change trades a state that retry repairs for one that only a command the author specifies as one‑shot can repair.

chunk_findings.detail: The removal decision was deliberately moved to a state folded under the lock (`fresh = fold(log.read_all(), ...)`), with the explicit rationale that state changed since `_load` must be seen. But the reply still reports the pre-lock record: `fix_task=rec.fix_task`, while `fix_task_removed=removed` is computed from `fresh`. Concretely: `bug invalid X` calls `_load`, observing X with no fix task (`rec.fix_task` empty/old). Before the command takes the transaction lock, the migration command in this same change (which files fix tasks for open bugs, `_file_fix_task`) files task `T` for still-open X, so the log now has X.fix_task = T. Under the lock, `fresh.bugs.get(bug, rec)` yields the fresh record, `_drop_fix_task` removes `T`, and the reply returns `fix_task_removed="T"` — but `fix_task` is still the stale `rec.fix_task` (empty, or an id that was already gone). The response therefore contradicts itself (`fix_task: null` yet a task was removed), and since the docstring states "the reply names it and the agent decides", the agent is told the wrong/nonexistent task. This should report `fresh.bugs.get(bug, rec).fix_task` to match the state the removal was actually decided from.

chunk_findings.detail: The new lift is `v.blockers = [b for b in v.blockers if not b.startswith(CM.OPEN_BUG_BLOCKER)]`, i.e. it drops *every* blocker produced by any open bug, not just the blockers for the bugs this item is actually closing. The comment right above it says "that one blocker... every other one still stands", and the `startswith` form (a prefix with a per-bug suffix) shows blockers are per-bug, so multiple can be present. The lift must be scoped to the bugs in `pending`; as written it also lifts the block a *different* open bug imposes on the same item's globs, which is exactly the "no bugs over bugs" guarantee the change is supposed to add. Concrete: `foo.py` has two open bugs B1 and B2, both filed against it; X1 is B1's fix task and inherits `foo.py` as its globs, so `CM.verdict` emits an OPEN_BUG_BLOCKER for B2 (B2 conflicts with X1's globs and X1 is not its fix task). Running `ddflow item complete X1 --regression-test test_b1` sets `closing=[test_b1]`, `pending=[B1]`; the comprehension strips B1's *and* B2's blockers, so X1 completes and merges a change to `foo.py` (closing only B1) while B2 is still open, instead of waiting as `v` demanded. Removing only `CM.OPEN_BUG_BLOCKER`-prefixed entries whose bug id is in `pending` would preserve "every other one still stands".

chunk_findings.detail: The `bug.found` event now records `fix_task = _fix_task_id(...)`, a *prediction* of the id `_file_fix_task` will bind, and the task is filed afterwards. The prediction is only correct for the two refusal cases that `_has_fix_task` models (an open bug-fix task named by `item`, or a live `fix-<bug>`). `_file_fix_task` has at least one other early return, visible in the same function body just below the new helpers: `src = st.items.get(item) if item else None; if src is not None and src.removed:`. When the bug’s `item` names an item that has been removed (and that removed item does not itself name an open bug-fix task), `_fix_task_id` returns `FIX_TASK_PREFIX + bug_id`, the bug event is appended with that id, and `_file_fix_task` then takes its removed-source path and does not file. Under the old code the bug’s `linked` came from the authoritative return value of `_file_fix_task` (`fix["fix_task"]`), which is empty on that path, so the bug carried no link; now the bug permanently names a task that does not exist. The comment’s proposed repair does not cover this: `bug file-tasks` re-derives the task by calling the same `_file_fix_task` over open bugs, hits the same `src.removed` path, and files nothing, so the dangling reference is never repaired. Trigger: `bug found --id B --item <removed-item>` (or the migration run over an open bug whose item was deleted while the bug stayed open). If the removed-source branch is instead meant to fall through and file the task, then it is not a defect — but that branch’s body is not part of this diff, and the code as shown introduces the divergence.

chunk_findings.detail: The handler deliberately re-folds the log under the lock (`fresh = fold(log.read_all(), strict=False)`) and computes the removal decision from that fresh state (`_drop_fix_task(log, fresh, fresh.bugs.get(bug, rec))`), precisely so that mutations made since `_load` are seen. But the newly added reply field is read from the *stale* record: `fix_task=rec.fix_task`. Concrete failure: while this caller holds a pre-lock `rec` with `fix_task == ""`, a concurrent `bug found` (or the one-shot migration) files fix task `T` for this same bug; `fresh.bugs[bug].fix_task == "T"`, and `_drop_fix_task` sees `T` as OPEN, unclaimed, named by no other open bug and needed by nobody, so it removes it and returns `"T"`. The reply then emits `fix_task=""` together with `fix_task_removed="T"` — a self-contradictory, stale description of the operation, even though the whole point of the fresh fold is to report/behave according to the current log. The value should come from the same record the decision was made on (`fresh.bugs.get(bug, rec).fix_task`).

chunk_findings.detail: `bug_fixed` is a persistence-mutating call: it closes the bug on disk and appends its own store/log events. The old code knew this and immediately refreshed after closing (`-        if closed: log, cfg, st = _load(repo, agent)`), precisely so the rest of `complete` operated on post-closure state. The new code deletes that refresh and moves the closure *after* the verdict, then continues to use the `log`/`st` snapshots that were loaded at the top of `complete` — `base["bugs_closed"] = closed`, `log.append("item.completed", ...)`, and the eventual persist all still write the pre-closure copies. Demonstrated input: bug B is filed with the default `[bugs] file_task = true`, giving fix task T (`B.fix_task == T`); run `ddflow item complete T --regression-test tests/test_b.py`. `pending == ["B"]`, the `OPEN_BUG_BLOCKER` is lifted, no other blocker remains, so the code proceeds to `bug_fixed(repo, "B", ...)`, which closes B; but because `st`/`log` were loaded before that call and are never reloaded, the subsequent `log.append`/save writes the snapshot in which B is still open (and `bug.fixed` is absent), silently undoing the closure that is the entire point of this change. The reload the diff removes is only correct to remove if `bug_fixed` no longer touched the shared store — which it clearly still does, since the old guard reloaded `log` and `st` immediately after it.

chunk_findings.detail: The new lift is `v.blockers = [b for b in v.blockers if not b.startswith(CM.OPEN_BUG_BLOCKER)]`, i.e. it drops *every* blocker produced by any open bug, not just the blockers for the bugs this item is actually closing. chunk_findings.detail: The new ordering writes the bug event — including `fix_task = fix-<bid>` — *before* `_file_fix_task` actually creates that task, and the only recovery the comment cites is the separate migration command `bug file-tasks`. That command is described in the intent as a one‑shot upgrade migration and nothing in `bug found`, `next` or `plan` invokes it, so the natural retry path no longer heals the state. Concretely: if `_file_fix_task` raises after the `bug.found` event has been durably appended (the code's own premise: "the lock is no rollback (each append is durable on its own)"), the command aborts with `B` recorded open and `fix_task=fix-B` pointing at a task that was never filed. Re‑running `bug found B` cannot repair it, because `prior = st.bugs.get(B)` is now non‑None, so `filing` is False, `linked` is empty and `_file_fix_task` is never called again — the bug is permanently without its fix task until an operator manually runs the migration. Under the old order the same crash (task appended, bug event not yet written) self‑healed: on retry `prior` was still None, `_file_fix_task` ran idempotently, found the already‑live `fix-B` via `_has_fix_task`, and the bug event was then written linking it. So the change trades a state that retry repairs for one that only a command the author specifies as one‑shot can repair.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge.py:_h_bug_found (the `log.append("bug.found", …)` now runs before `_file_fix_task`)

chunk_findings.detail: The removal decision was deliberately moved to a state folded under the lock (`fresh = fold(log.read_all(), ...)`), with the explicit rationale that state changed since `_load` must be seen. But the reply still reports the pre-lock record: `fix_task=rec.fix_task`, while `fix_task_removed=removed` is computed from `fresh`. Concretely: `bug invalid X` calls `_load`, observing X with no fix task (`rec.fix_task` empty/old). Before the command takes the transaction lock, the migration command in this same change (which files fix tasks for open bugs, `_file_fix_task`) files task `T` for still-open X, so the log now has X.fix_task = T. Under the lock, `fresh.bugs.get(bug, rec)` yields the fresh record, `_drop_fix_task` removes `T`, and the reply returns `fix_task_removed="T"` — but `fix_task` is still the stale `rec.fix_task` (empty, or an id that was already gone). The response therefore contradicts itself (`fix_task: null` yet a task was removed), and since the docstring states "the reply names it and the agent decides", the agent is told the wrong/nonexistent task. This should report `fresh.bugs.get(bug, rec).fix_task` to match the state the removal was actually decided from.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge.py (`fix_task=rec.fix_task` in the `bug.invalid` reply)

chunk_findings.detail: The new lift is `v.blockers = [b for b in v.blockers if not b.startswith(CM.OPEN_BUG_BLOCKER)]`, i.e. it drops *every* blocker produced by any open bug, not just the blockers for the bugs this item is actually closing. The comment right above it says "that one blocker... every other one still stands", and the `startswith` form (a prefix with a per-bug suffix) shows blockers are per-bug, so multiple can be present. The lift must be scoped to the bugs in `pending`; as written it also lifts the block a *different* open bug imposes on the same item's globs, which is exactly the "no bugs over bugs" guarantee the change is supposed to add. Concrete: `foo.py` has two open bugs B1 and B2, both filed against it; X1 is B1's fix task and inherits `foo.py` as its globs, so `CM.verdict` emits an OPEN_BUG_BLOCKER for B2 (B2 conflicts with X1's globs and X1 is not its fix task). Running `ddflow item complete X1 --regression-test test_b1` sets `closing=[test_b1]`, `pending=[B1]`; the comprehension strips B1's *and* B2's blockers, so X1 completes and merges a change to `foo.py` (closing only B1) while B2 is still open, instead of waiting as `v` demanded. Removing only `CM.OPEN_BUG_BLOCKER`-prefixed entries whose bug id is in `pending` would preserve "every other one still stands".
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle.py:1416

chunk_findings.detail: The new "is the record's fix task missing?" test is evaluated against `st` as loaded by `_load` *before* `with log.transaction():` (line 555), not against a state refolded under the lock. The sibling code the same change touches (`bug invalid`, line ~925) explicitly refolds under the lock for exactly this reason ("a claim on the fix task made since `_load` must be seen, or the task is removed under its holder"), so the pattern is the intended one and this call site violates it. Concretely: bug B is open with `fix_task="fix-B"` but no `fix-B` item in the queue (the crash case the change exists to repair). Process P1 runs `bug file-tasks`; inside its lock it folds, sees B dangling, files `fix-B`, and (say) an agent claims it, then commits. Process P2 simultaneously runs `bug found` for B; its `_load` ran before P1 committed, so its `st` still lacks `fix-B`, `_live(st, "fix-B")` returns False, `dangling` is True, and `filing` is True (line 548). When P2's transaction acquires the lock it proceeds to append a create for `fix-B` again even though the fresh log already has a live, claimed `fix-B`. Depending on how the fold applies a second create for an existing id, this either duplicates the task or clobbers the claim/state that P1's write installed — the exact "removed under its holder" failure the `bug invalid` path guards against. The same stale-state window applies to a concurrent `bug file-tasks`/`bug found` pair. The check needs the same refold-under-the-lock the `bug invalid` path uses.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/knowledge.py:548 (`dangling`/`filing` in `bug found`)

chunk_findings.detail: The test codifies that when the item a bug names has been removed, the filed fix task gets `globs == []` (and the standing `bugs` parent), i.e. removal deliberately *stops glob inheritance*. That contradicts the change's own stated intent (a) "globs given **or inherited from that item**" and (c) "a feature touching the same globs waits (glob conflict) — no bugs over bugs". Concretely: if `F1` (phase `P1`, globs e.g. `src/parser.py`) is dropped and a real bug is reported against it, `bug_found(..., item="F1")` here yields `items["fix-Bx"].globs == []`, so a concurrently planned feature that touches `src/parser.py` will *not* be forced to wait behind the bugfix. The one mechanism the change adds to prevent bugs accumulating over the files where bugs live is disabled for exactly the bugs whose source item is gone, which is when the fix task most needs to guard those files. Either the fix task should inherit the removed item's globs (and only fall back to the standing `bugs` phase for the parent), or the test's expectation/comment is wrong; as written the test enshrines a hole in the "no bugs over bugs" guarantee.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewrite drops the entire sentence "*closing it and opening two new ones instead would lose the thread between what was planned and what happened*". The remaining text ("Split an item into sub-tasks IN PLACE … The original keeps its id and history and becomes an umbrella that completes when its children do") states where the work goes, but no longer states *why* closing the item and opening two fresh ones is wrong — the loss of the plan-vs-actual link. That rationale is precisely the argument the consumer agent weighs when choosing `ddflow_split` over a close + two `ddflow_add` calls, so its removal is a lost meaning, not a shortening, and it contradicts the change's stated constraint that "every meaning kept". The other compressions in this diff (e.g. `globs`, `pr_sync`, `parent`) preserve the corresponding claims; this one does not.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:625 (`ddflow_split` description)

chunk_findings.detail: The rewrite drops a whole piece of call-time guidance that the stated intent ("what the tool does, when to call it … every meaning kept") promises to preserve. The original read: "Prefer this to a remembered rule whenever the pattern is mechanical: a count says 'worse' and never 'which' …". The new text keeps only the rationale fragment — "(a count says 'worse', never 'which')" — and deletes the sentence that actually tells the agent *when* to supply `pattern` instead of a remembered rule. The consequence is concrete: an agent that is deciding whether to pass a mechanical regex or write a prose "how" now sees only "A regex naming the mistake in CODE. Scans the repository now and stores WHICH sites match…", with no instruction that this is the preferred path for mechanical mistakes, so it can legitimately fall back to a remembered rule and lose the "which sites" inventory the tool exists to produce. The `supersedes`, `apply` and `ddflow_cleanup` edits in this hunk do preserve their meaning; this one does not.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:748 ("pattern" param of ddflow_lesson_add)

chunk_findings.detail: The stated intent is that every meaning is kept. The rewritten description silently drops the glossary for the `flags` field and the enumeration of `state` values that the old text supplied, and those are the only places a caller could learn what the field contents mean. Old text: `state (open, claimed by whom, done, fixed, invalid, removed...)` and `flags (identical text; the text names its id)`. New text: just `state` and just `flags`. A consumer that receives a record with `flags` set (e.g. the "identical text" flag) now has no way from this description to know what the flag signifies, and no way to know the possible `state` strings; the old description told it. This contradicts the "shorten descriptions only, every meaning kept" premise of the change, since `flags` in particular was only meaningful because of the deleted parenthetical.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow_similar (ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py, description)

chunk_findings.detail: The shortened subagent clause now reads "...it passes `as_agent` on each call instead (every tool takes it; same name rules; the CLI's `--agent`)". The original said "every other tool takes it" — the word *other* was doing real work: it excluded `ddflow_identify` itself, which is the one tool whose only declared parameter here is `agent` (the `properties` block in this same diff lists just `"agent"`, with no `as_agent`). The new wording asserts the opposite, and it does so in the same sentence that forbids a subagent from calling this tool. A subagent that shares its parent's connection and reads "every tool takes it" has no way to know `as_agent` is not accepted by `ddflow_identify`; if it passes `as_agent` to this tool (or infers that identity can be re-attributed per call on the connection tool), the call is not supported by the schema shown here — the very confusion the original "every other tool" phrasing was written to prevent. This is a meaning change, not a shortening: the tool's parameter surface is misdescribed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py — `ddflow_identify` description ("every tool takes it")

chunk_findings.detail: The pre-change description contained a rationale sentence — "A queue that starts empty tells you nothing is in flight about a project that may have three branches in flight." — that is entirely absent from the replacement text. The retained sentence ("Call it right after `ddflow_setup` on any repository that is not brand new") still says *when* to call, but the merged paragraph now drops the reason the caller should trust that cue: that an empty queue on a history-bearing repo is misleading rather than evidence of a clean project. This is the one client-visible meaning removed by this part and it conflicts with the change's stated intent that "when to call it" be preserved. Every other edit here (status, sources, verify, apply/out params) is a faithful compression: defaults, exit code 2, the "writes NOTHING until `apply` is true" refusal, and the "GUESS about structure" caveat all survive with the same meaning.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py ddflow_import description

chunk_findings.detail: The original described the returned command as "the project's own test command with its runner and worker flags, the files swapped in". The replacement keeps only "with the project's own runner flags", dropping both the worker-flag requirement that makes the parallel run actually parallel (e.g. pytest `-n auto`, `--workers`) and the fact that the selected test files are substituted into the project's command. A caller following the new text has no instruction to set worker flags and no statement that the command runs only the reached tests, so it can emit a command that either runs serially or runs the project's default test set (e.g. the whole suite) instead of the listed files — behavior the old text explicitly specified. The intent states every meaning is kept, and this is the part of the description that defines what the tool returns.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py — `ddflow_tests` description (hunk at `@@ -1921,15 +1728,7 @@`)

chunk_findings.detail: The shortened description collapses the TOML example onto one line: `` `toml` APPENDS a fragment, e.g. [gate.unit_tests] command = "pytest -q -n auto" ...``. The removed version was a two-line example (`[gate.unit_tests]\n  command = "pytest -q -n auto"\n`), whose newline is what makes it valid TOML. A table header must be followed by a newline; `[a] b = 1` on a single line is a syntax error in every conforming parser (CPython `tomllib` raises `TOMLDecodeError: Expected newline or end of document after a statement`). So a caller that reproduces the example literally, e.g. `ddflow_configure(toml='[gate.unit_tests] command = "pytest -q -n auto"')`, gets a config.toml fragment that cannot be parsed back — the very "prints every knob" path the description describes would then fail. The example presented in the description no longer demonstrates a usable input, which is a meaning the old text conveyed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:1812 (`ddflow_configure` description)

chunk_findings.detail: The original ended with the caller-facing rule "Declare it for anything that starts a GPU job, a model server or a long run." The new text stops at the format example (`'gpu:4,vllm-fleet'`) and the scheduler sentence; the entire when-to-declare instruction is gone. A caller who only reads the description now has no statement that resources must be declared for GPU jobs / model servers / long runs, which is exactly the "when to call it" meaning the change claims to preserve. Nothing else in the string conveys it (the parenthetical "[schedule] resources" only names the config section).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:2026 (update `resources` property description)

chunk_findings.detail: The original stated the concrete lease behavior "re-claiming keeps the item's recorded tree" as the explanation of "the way out of a binding to the wrong tree". The new string deletes that clause and leaves "…the way out of a binding to the wrong tree; merge then lands that tree's branch." A caller now reads that the way out is tied to merge landing the tree's branch, with no statement that re-claiming intentionally retains the recorded tree — i.e. the refusal/behavior fact that explains *why* re-claiming cannot rebind the item is removed, and the surviving clause is misleading about the mechanism.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:2032 (update `worktree` property description)

chunk_findings.detail: Original: "Use it instead of polling or asking the operator when a claim was refused…"; new: "Use it instead of polling when a claim was refused…". The "or asking the operator" alternative is dropped, so the guidance about which human-escalation path this tool replaces no longer appears in the description.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:2130 (`ddflow_wait` description)

chunk_findings.detail: The old text promised the detached session outlives "you, this server **and a restarted remote-control service**"; the new text says only "so it outlives you and this server". The remote-control service is a distinct, separately-restartable process, and its restart is exactly the scenario that motivates detaching. An agent reading the new description can only conclude a job dies when the remote-control service restarts, so for a long training run it may either decline to launch it at all or re-launch a duplicate after a restart — while the job is in fact still alive. That is a behavioral change driven purely by the dropped clause, and it is not compensated anywhere else in the new sentence.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:2201 (`ddflow_job_run` description)

chunk_findings.detail: Two operative pieces of the old `lost`/`refile_as` sentence were dropped: "re-add it **under a new id**" and "**or it exists only in the log**". The first told the caller the refile must use a fresh id; the second told the caller the consequence of not refiling, i.e. the losing definition is otherwise reachable only in the log and not as a live item. With input "resolve a contested item whose losing definition is real, then omit `refile_as`", an agent using the shortened text has no statement that the definition ceases to exist as a usable item, which is precisely the failure the sentence existed to prevent.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewrite drops the entire sentence "*closing it and opening two new ones instead would lose the thread between what was planned and what happened*". The remaining text ("Split an item into sub-tasks IN PLACE … The original keeps its id and history and becomes an umbrella that completes when its children do") states where the work goes, but no longer states *why* closing the item and opening two fresh ones is wrong — the loss of the plan-vs-actual link. That rationale is precisely the argument the consumer agent weighs when choosing `ddflow_split` over a close + two `ddflow_add` calls, so its removal is a lost meaning, not a shortening, and it contradicts the change's stated constraint that "every meaning kept". The other compressions in this diff (e.g. `globs`, `pr_sync`, `parent`) preserve the corresponding claims; this one does not.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:625 (`ddflow_split` description)

chunk_findings.detail: The rewrite drops a whole piece of call-time guidance that the stated intent ("what the tool does, when to call it … every meaning kept") promises to preserve. The original read: "Prefer this to a remembered rule whenever the pattern is mechanical: a count says 'worse' and never 'which' …". The new text keeps only the rationale fragment — "(a count says 'worse', never 'which')" — and deletes the sentence that actually tells the agent *when* to supply `pattern` instead of a remembered rule. The consequence is concrete: an agent that is deciding whether to pass a mechanical regex or write a prose "how" now sees only "A regex naming the mistake in CODE. Scans the repository now and stores WHICH sites match…", with no instruction that this is the preferred path for mechanical mistakes, so it can legitimately fall back to a remembered rule and lose the "which sites" inventory the tool exists to produce. The `supersedes`, `apply` and `ddflow_cleanup` edits in this hunk do preserve their meaning; this one does not.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:748 ("pattern" param of ddflow_lesson_add)

chunk_findings.detail: The stated intent is that every meaning is kept. The rewritten description silently drops the glossary for the `flags` field and the enumeration of `state` values that the old text supplied, and those are the only places a caller could learn what the field contents mean. Old text: `state (open, claimed by whom, done, fixed, invalid, removed...)` and `flags (identical text; the text names its id)`. New text: just `state` and just `flags`. A consumer that receives a record with `flags` set (e.g. the "identical text" flag) now has no way from this description to know what the flag signifies, and no way to know the possible `state` strings; the old description told it. This contradicts the "shorten descriptions only, every meaning kept" premise of the change, since `flags` in particular was only meaningful because of the deleted parenthetical.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow_similar (ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py, description)

chunk_findings.detail: The shortened subagent clause now reads "...it passes `as_agent` on each call instead (every tool takes it; same name rules; the CLI's `--agent`)". The original said "every other tool takes it" — the word *other* was doing real work: it excluded `ddflow_identify` itself, which is the one tool whose only declared parameter here is `agent` (the `properties` block in this same diff lists just `"agent"`, with no `as_agent`). The new wording asserts the opposite, and it does so in the same sentence that forbids a subagent from calling this tool. A subagent that shares its parent's connection and reads "every tool takes it" has no way to know `as_agent` is not accepted by `ddflow_identify`; if it passes `as_agent` to this tool (or infers that identity can be re-attributed per call on the connection tool), the call is not supported by the schema shown here — the very confusion the original "every other tool" phrasing was written to prevent. This is a meaning change, not a shortening: the tool's parameter surface is misdescribed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py — `ddflow_identify` description ("every tool takes it")

chunk_findings.detail: The pre-change description contained a rationale sentence — "A queue that starts empty tells you nothing is in flight about a project that may have three branches in flight." — that is entirely absent from the replacement text. The retained sentence ("Call it right after `ddflow_setup` on any repository that is not brand new") still says *when* to call, but the merged paragraph now drops the reason the caller should trust that cue: that an empty queue on a history-bearing repo is misleading rather than evidence of a clean project. This is the one client-visible meaning removed by this part and it conflicts with the change's stated intent that "when to call it" be preserved. Every other edit here (status, sources, verify, apply/out params) is a faithful compression: defaults, exit code 2, the "writes NOTHING until `apply` is true" refusal, and the "GUESS about structure" caveat all survive with the same meaning.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py ddflow_import description

chunk_findings.detail: The original described the returned command as "the project's own test command with its runner and worker flags, the files swapped in". The replacement keeps only "with the project's own runner flags", dropping both the worker-flag requirement that makes the parallel run actually parallel (e.g. pytest `-n auto`, `--workers`) and the fact that the selected test files are substituted into the project's command. A caller following the new text has no instruction to set worker flags and no statement that the command runs only the reached tests, so it can emit a command that either runs serially or runs the project's default test set (e.g. the whole suite) instead of the listed files — behavior the old text explicitly specified. The intent states every meaning is kept, and this is the part of the description that defines what the tool returns.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py — `ddflow_tests` description (hunk at `@@ -1921,15 +1728,7 @@`)

chunk_findings.detail: The shortened description collapses the TOML example onto one line: `` `toml` APPENDS a fragment, e.g. [gate.unit_tests] command = "pytest -q -n auto" ...``. The removed version was a two-line example (`[gate.unit_tests]\n  command = "pytest -q -n auto"\n`), whose newline is what makes it valid TOML. A table header must be followed by a newline; `[a] b = 1` on a single line is a syntax error in every conforming parser (CPython `tomllib` raises `TOMLDecodeError: Expected newline or end of document after a statement`). So a caller that reproduces the example literally, e.g. `ddflow_configure(toml='[gate.unit_tests] command = "pytest -q -n auto"')`, gets a config.toml fragment that cannot be parsed back — the very "prints every knob" path the description describes would then fail. The example presented in the description no longer demonstrates a usable input, which is a meaning the old text conveyed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:1812 (`ddflow_configure` description)

chunk_findings.detail: The original ended with the caller-facing rule "Declare it for anything that starts a GPU job, a model server or a long run." The new text stops at the format example (`'gpu:4,vllm-fleet'`) and the scheduler sentence; the entire when-to-declare instruction is gone. A caller who only reads the description now has no statement that resources must be declared for GPU jobs / model servers / long runs, which is exactly the "when to call it" meaning the change claims to preserve. Nothing else in the string conveys it (the parenthetical "[schedule] resources" only names the config section).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:2026 (update `resources` property description)

chunk_findings.detail: The original stated the concrete lease behavior "re-claiming keeps the item's recorded tree" as the explanation of "the way out of a binding to the wrong tree". The new string deletes that clause and leaves "…the way out of a binding to the wrong tree; merge then lands that tree's branch." A caller now reads that the way out is tied to merge landing the tree's branch, with no statement that re-claiming intentionally retains the recorded tree — i.e. the refusal/behavior fact that explains *why* re-claiming cannot rebind the item is removed, and the surviving clause is misleading about the mechanism.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:2032 (update `worktree` property description)

chunk_findings.detail: Original: "Use it instead of polling or asking the operator when a claim was refused…"; new: "Use it instead of polling when a claim was refused…". The "or asking the operator" alternative is dropped, so the guidance about which human-escalation path this tool replaces no longer appears in the description.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:2130 (`ddflow_wait` description)

chunk_findings.detail: The old text promised the detached session outlives "you, this server **and a restarted remote-control service**"; the new text says only "so it outlives you and this server". The remote-control service is a distinct, separately-restartable process, and its restart is exactly the scenario that motivates detaching. An agent reading the new description can only conclude a job dies when the remote-control service restarts, so for a long training run it may either decline to launch it at all or re-launch a duplicate after a restart — while the job is in fact still alive. That is a behavioral change driven purely by the dropped clause, and it is not compensated anywhere else in the new sentence.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:2201 (`ddflow_job_run` description)

chunk_findings.detail: Two operative pieces of the old `lost`/`refile_as` sentence were dropped: "re-add it **under a new id**" and "**or it exists only in the log**". The first told the caller the refile must use a fresh id; the second told the caller the consequence of not refiling, i.e. the losing definition is otherwise reachable only in the log and not as a live item. With input "resolve a contested item whose losing definition is real, then omit `refile_as`", an agent using the shortened text has no statement that the definition ceases to exist as a usable item, which is precisely the failure the sentence existed to prevent.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/mcp.py:2344 (`ddflow_resolve` description)

chunk_findings.detail: The old text was `"Treat query as a regular expression (default false)."`; the new text is `"Treat the query as a regular expression."`, so the documented default of `false` is gone. This is the only parameter in the `ddflow_rule_search` block whose default was deleted — `exact` immediately above it still reads `"Exact phrase match (default false)."` and `limit` still reads `"(default 10)"` — so the schema is now self-inconsistent: a caller that reads the same tool's descriptions learns the default for `exact` but not for `regex`. Given the stated intent ("Restore ... the twelve meanings the first review found dropped, and pay for the bytes on the rule tools' parameter texts"), the byte saving on this parameter was taken by re-dropping one of the meanings the change was supposed to restore, so a model that omits `regex` (the common case) has no documented way to know whether the query will be interpreted as a literal string or a regex. Restore the `(default false)` suffix (or state the default elsewhere in the description) while spending the saved bytes on a different, non-meaning-bearing string.
